description: It is centrally positioned, as it is strongly linked to the surrounding others. It is the evolution of the fathers’ cluster solely focused on networks. Here the topic can be summarized as the need for the FF to exploit its personal ties in order to enter a new foreign market and overcome uncertainty and local cultural differences (e.g. Reuber 2016). This group of papers mainly employs the SEW approach, which is why this group of scholars give so much relevance to trust and family ties to internationalize business (e.g. Cesinger et al. 2016). The central position of this cluster is explained by the commonality of topics shared with other papers that are more strongly focused on other subjects and thus included in different clusters. For instance, the work of Stieg et al. (2017) is focused on networks but also on generational and managerial features influencing internationalization (which is why this paper is closed to both the clear blue and the green cluster). In the same vein, Reuber (2016) is positioned at the bottom of the map, as it is mainly focused on networks but also interested in decision processes (which is why the paper is also close to the yellow cluster); or the reason why Mensching et al. (2016) are mainly interested in cultural distance but also on CEO characteristics (which is why the paper is also closed to the clear blue cluster).

It is on the top left-hand corner and the papers are focused on individuals who sit on the board and influence internationalization choices. The academic debate is herein concentrated on understanding if, and in which amount, external managers should be involved in the board or on understanding if family members’ participation in the board may influence the internationalization success (e.g. D’Angelo et al. 2016).

It is a very small cluster positioned on the top right-hand corner, based on upper echelons (Hambrick and Mason 1984) and focused on a new topic if compared to fathers. For instance, Ramón-Llorens et al. (2017) focused on the demographic variables, gender, and CEO academic level of achievements as crucial factors influencing the success of IFB. The same for Almodovar et al. (2016) who focused on human asset qualities of IFB. Both papers are physically close to the violet cluster, as they also look at the presence of such individuals within the board.

It is on the bottom left hand corner and is mainly focused on the context (e.g. Kostova and Hult 2016) of internationalization and, more specifically, on the factors favoring internationalization (e.g. Lehrer and Celo 2017) or, for instance, the country-level factors affecting export intensity (i.e. Carney et  al. 2017). Thus, they employ various theoretical frameworks, such as the institutional framework (e.g. Hung and Tseng 2017; Kostova and Hult 2016), the Ownership-Location-Internalization (OLI) framework to stress the location-specific advantages of the international expansion, and the resource-based view (e.g. Chung and Dahms 2016).

It is on right-hand corner and papers herein employ the resource-based view or resource dependency (e.g. Singh and Kota 2017) as the approaches that can best explain the innovativeness of IFB, and the international entrepreneurship orientation as the main factor contributing to international success (e.g. Bettinelli et al. 2017). For instance, Braga et al. (2017) stress that only few papers syndicate the relationship between innovation and internationalization. In this regard, Calabrò et al. (2016b) found a direct relationship between innovativeness and international venturing moderated by family ownership. Also, Singh and Kota (2017) found that IFB are more innovative and internationalized than non-IFB and that such difference is even larger when the IFB are younger and smaller compared to older and bigger pairs.

It is positioned at the center and bottom of the map and focuses on the decision process required to individuate opportunities in IFB. Key in this regard are Tegtmeier and Classen (2017) who conceptually syndicate if such recognition by IFB differs from non-IFB, or Zaefarian et al. (2016) who explain how IFB engage in a systematic search for information to reduce international risk. Also, Laffranchini et  al. (2016) focus on the cognitive processes required to discover and exploit international opportunities; and Ratten and Tajeddini (2017) detect innovativeness as the result of opportunity identification. Interestingly, Calabrò et al. (2016b) location on the map is very close to the clear blue cluster, as they also focus on the generation running the IFB.
